paragraphs.text: Made, likely, or rather made use of from Psa 40:14-15, &c., when Sheba, the son of Bichri, was up in rebellion after Absalom’s death, 2Sa 20:1, &c. See Psa 69:1, title.

Worthy to be remembered, and followed as a pattern of prayer. Some make this psalm an appendix to the former, as Psa 43:1-5., is to Psa 42:1-11. Others make it a part of the next psalm; which is, therefore, say they, without a title.
As a father runs without legs when his child is hazarded.
paragraphs.anchor: Make haste, O God, to deliver me

paragraphs.text: Vel sicut per insidias vel supplantationem, more athletarum, a ò÷á, Let them be supplanted, defeated.
paragraphs.anchor: Let them be turned back for a reward

paragraphs.text: That say, Aha, aha] Augustine rendereth it, Euge, Euge, that is, Well done; and giveth this note upon it, Plus persequitur lingua adulatoris quam manus interfectoris, The tongue of a flatterer may mischief a man more than the hand of a murderer. The apostle, Heb 11:37, ranketh their tempting and flattering promises among their bloody deeds, their rising tongues with their terrifying jaws.
Piorum characteres, saith one, a godly man characterized, by his search after God, his joy in him, his love to him, his praises of him.
paragraphs.anchor: Let all those that seek thee, &c.

paragraphs.text: In illo quicquid ego; ille, non ego, saith Augustine.

paragraphs.anchor: But I am poor and needy
